source_type_decision.reason: Both restored source rows ask the same broad Linux common-command concept question. The normalized canonical narrows the useful interview scope to online troubleshooting, so a qualifying answer should organize commands by diagnostic purpose, explain how observations narrow the search space, state interpretation boundaries, and remain orally usable rather than become an unstructured command catalog.

primary_sources_checked.title: The /proc Filesystem — Linux Kernel documentation
verified_claims: procfs exposes process and system state used by monitoring and diagnosis, including load and task-related information
procfs data is an observation source that must be interpreted in the relevant process/system scope

primary_sources_checked.title: proc_loadavg(5) — Linux man-pages
verified_claims: Linux load average accounts for runnable tasks and tasks in uninterruptible sleep, so it is not equivalent to CPU utilization

primary_sources_checked.title: PSI - Pressure Stall Information — Linux Kernel documentation
verified_claims: PSI exposes CPU, memory and I/O pressure through /proc/pressure
pressure metrics quantify workload stall impact from resource contention rather than merely reporting capacity totals

primary_sources_checked.title: Control Group v2 — Linux Kernel documentation
verified_claims: cgroup v2 provides scoped memory usage, event and pressure interfaces such as memory.current, memory.events and memory.pressure

primary_sources_checked.title: iostat manual — sysstat upstream
verified_claims: the first iostat report normally covers time since system startup while subsequent reports cover the interval since the preceding report; -y omits the first report
%util near 100% is a saturation indication for devices that serve requests serially, but it does not express the performance limit of parallel devices such as RAID arrays and modern SSDs

primary_sources_checked.title: sar manual — sysstat upstream
verified_claims: sar can collect, save and later report system activity records, so retrospective incident analysis depends on collection having been configured and retained

primary_sources_checked.title: strace project documentation
verified_claims: strace traces system calls and signals and is appropriate as a scoped process-level diagnostic tool rather than a first-step global monitor

primary_sources_checked.title: Perf events and tool security — Linux Kernel documentation
verified_claims: performance-monitoring data can expose sensitive execution information and therefore requires an explicit access and production-safety boundary

findings.finding: The candidate directly answers the restored Linux common-command source rows through the canonical online-troubleshooting scope and uses each command as evidence in a narrowing diagnostic flow instead of drifting into the prior generic system-design template.
Load average is correctly separated from CPU utilization and cross-checked against CPU count, runnable/blocked tasks and pressure evidence, avoiding the common single-metric diagnosis error.
The iostat section correctly states first-report sampling semantics and preserves the upstream modern SSD/RAID boundary for %util instead of treating 100% as a universal storage saturation threshold.
The answer distinguishes host totals from cgroup-scoped memory accounting and PSI pressure, which is necessary for container/resource-limit diagnosis.

Historical sar use is conditional on retained collection data, strace/perf are scoped as deeper probes with operational and sensitive-data boundaries, and the project section explicitly refuses to invent incident metrics or outcomes.
